subject: literature
passage: A great many novels published in Britain during the nineteenth century appeared anonymously or under a pen name, so reviewers often had to guess at the author's identity, and in particular at the author's sex. Literary historian Joanna Reyes argues that those guesses governed the verdicts. Qualities that reviewers admired as vigorous and frank in a book they believed to be a man's, she contends, were condemned as coarse and improper when the same reviewers believed a book to be a woman's; the words on the page mattered less than the sex the reviewer had assigned to the hand that wrote them.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Reyes's argument?

choices.A: Reviewers applied the same standards to anonymous novels whether or not they took the author to be a woman, and said so in their reviews.
choices.B: Reviewers of the period guessed wrongly about the sex of anonymous authors in a large share of cases, and often admitted as much in print.
choices.C: After a novel reviewed as a man's work was revealed to be by a woman, reviews of its next edition condemned as unsuitable the very scenes the earlier reviews had admired for their frankness.
choices.D: Novels known to be by women sold in numbers comparable to novels known to be by men throughout the period.

explanation.why: Reyes's claim is that the same text drew different verdicts depending on the sex reviewers assigned to its author. The cleanest support holds the text constant and changes only the assumed sex. Reviews of the same scenes turning from admiration to condemnation once the author was known to be a woman is exactly that comparison.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Reviewers using the same standards regardless of assumed sex is the opposite of what Reyes claims.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Reviewers guessing wrongly shows that they guessed, but not that their guesses changed how they judged a book.
explanation.C: Correct. The same scenes judged differently once the author's sex was known shows that the assumed sex, not the text, drove the verdict.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Sales reflect readers' choices, not how reviewers judged the writing.
